text:
It definitely appears to be underpowered. Assuming there should be a reasonably linear improvement among the Nvidia cards:

1080p fps Game Average
3080 to 3070 = 19 fps drop. 3070 to 3060 = 39 fps drop.
2080 to 2070 = 24 fps drop. 2070 to 2060 = 13 fps drop.

1440p fps Game Average
3080 to 3070 = 26 fps drop. 3070 to 3060 = 35 fps drop.
2080 to 2070 = 21 fps drop. 2070 to 2060 = 12 fps drop.

So the drop from xx70 to xx60 is 3 times worse for the 30xx cards, whereas the drop between xx80 to xx70 is similar for both generations.
In other words, stay away from the 3060 unless you are desperate. The 3060Ti is about right.

Nvidia recently reported a $5Bn quarterly revenue last quarter, its biggest ever. In 12 months time, we'll all be on the hype train for the 40xx cards and the many reviews of 30xx cards will have achieved nothing for gamers.

It galls me that they are making such massive profits while claiming they cannot supply gamers with cards. Why are we supporting these companies by continuing to hype them up? I wish everybody would either stop talking about GPUs completely or only when directing angry comments at AMD/Nvidia. Negative publicity can really hurt the decision makers in these companies and frankly that's the only way we're going to get cards this side of Christmas.

@Icetea-2000  apart from the 3060, I'd definitely consider it, mainly as my current card is 'very' old.

But if I currently had anything from a 1070, 1080/Ti, a 2070, or 5700XT, then there's no way I'd pay even MSRP for these and I don't think they're a "good deal" by any means, except perhaps compared to Turing (very low bar)

since Pascal, Nvidia's shifted the Overton window of what 'midrange' pricing means. Compare the card prices at each tier from 2008-2017, then 2018-present (post-cryptoboom)

What almost every previous generation did was improve or maintain performance for the same price point, and more drastically over time than between Pascal & Ampere too.

Turing changed everything. They improved performance (less than average), but they also increased prices proportionately to that performance increase. So effectively you were paying the same cost per frame, they just let you pay even more.

That's why a 3070 for $499 is not a good deal. if you take the 1070's launch MSRP & account for inflation, it'd be $413 today. The 970 would be $364. Even the 1070Ti would be $479. Going back to the upper midrange of 2008 the 9800GT would only be $270 in today's money.

And that's without getting into how cards also previously dropped "below" their MSRP after 6 months or so as yields improved, not maintained or increased it.

So Nvidia has effectively moved prices up a bracket or two in real terms even accounting for inflation. AMD has followed suit because undercutting Nvidia's price:performance didn't actually gain them market share in the past, now everything they're putting out is selling anyway and they have a lot of financial ground to make up to be able to afford to be more competitive with Nvidia in other aspects of their business & software stack.

TLDR: I would, but I still wouldn't be happy about a '70 class card costing $500

However, cards have also become relatively more powerful even compared to their time. Ever noticed how framerates in benchmarks have changed since like 2012 for example? Back then cards were usually from 30-60 fps even at the high end, and that was in contemporary games. Today, even low end cards are easily able to hit 100+ fps in 1080p in some titles. The whole market shifted towards getting a whole more frames per second as a standard base line, 30 fps usually is seen as not good enough while 60 fps is only labeled as comfortably playable, whereas it was among the best back in the day. 

So while yes, I agree they should just adjust their naming scheme, the demands have disproportionately gone up as well. I like AMDs way of basically adding a new "level" of cards as the 800 series above the previous high end of AMD being the 700 series. All the while still releasing a 6700xt for the newest generation, so it doesn’t feel like you need to pay more for the same category, but more for an entirely higher level of performance, while there is still the 700 series to compare the 5700xt to. 

I hope I properly explained what I mean
author: @Icetea-2000

text:
@Icetea-2000  I get what you mean but I have to reject those terms. Because the increase in performance standards is also nothing new. The standard used to be 720p and 1024z768, 1280x1024 & 1600x1200 in the PC space, then 1080p became standard, then 60fps became standard, then 1440p. And throughout all that the price range for the stack remained close to the same.

Not only that, but compering the performance uplift gen on gen in absolute terms with like-for-like benchmarks & settings, there's been no radical increase in performance there either compared with gains in the past.

That sort of thing is a rational sounding misdirection. Keep your mind on what the performance gain for the same games at the same settings and resolution is. Now compare this to the gains we got in the past.

There is no equivalency at all. performance increases are not outpacing price increases to remotely the same degree as previously with Pascal over Maxwell over Kepler.

Also I'll draw your attention to the PS5 & the Series X. Look at Digital Foundry's videos on what PC you need for equivalent performance at equivalent settings. It varies considerably of course but in almost all cases, the GPU you need to match the performance at equivalent settings, costs as much as the entire console themselves, even at MSRP. In real terms, the GPUs sell for far more.

Now the consoles have a lot more in them. Their CPU is a stripped back 5700x. They have a 1TB nvme drive that retails for well over $100 for PC equivalents. The PSU  mobo, case, heatsink, controller, packaging - none of that comes free.

Now the upcoming RX6700XT is likely going to have similar performance to the Series X, but I can tell you right now they'll be selling on ebay at over $650 within a week of launch.

Now what does this tell you? Because it tells me that AMD and Nvidia are both making insane profit margins even at MSRP let-alone  what they'll wind up going for - because demand is so insanely high.

Ultimately the fact is that the cost to manufacture GPUs hasn't gone up by much even with covid effecting supply lines. The prices have gone up, because enough people out there will pay them.

My previous upgrade path was:

2008 - 9800GT - $230
2011 - GTX 560 Ti - $250 
2014 - GTX 970 - $330

Each of the above cards tripled the performance of the previous one if you care to look into the benchmarks of the time.

Going by MSRP alone, I don't even get remotely close to another upgrade on relative performance by price like this until the RTX 3070 (and probably RX6700XT).
